other_side: Zitron's data centre argument is not about whether communities should be angry — it is about whether the thing they are being asked to host will still be running to pay them. He counts roughly 190 gigawatts of capacity in planning, implying about $1.68 trillion of annual compute revenue to justify it, against genuine demand he puts nearer $120 billion a year, 70 to 90 per cent of it from two loss-making labs. Each site is financed inside its own special purpose vehicle that services debt only out of customer revenue, so on his reading "the vast majority of AI data centers and their associated SPVs will collapse" if that demand never arrives. He restated the demand half of it as recently as 11 August. Where NLW sees Loudoun County's tax base and Quincy's swimming pool as the template, Zitron would say those were built on demand that already existed — and that a town signing a twenty-year bargain with an SPV in 2026 is counterparty to a balance sheet, not to Microsoft.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is durability of the local bargain: not whether a data centre is worth hosting today, but whether the entity promising the taxes, the grid payments and the park is still solvent to deliver them in ten years. Both accept the sites are being built at extraordinary speed, that the money behind them is largely debt, and that host communities currently negotiate in the dark. The empirical question that will resolve is whether newly energised capacity gets contracted — the observable is occupancy and lease renewal at the 2026-27 cohort of sites, and whether any sizeable data centre SPV defaults or is restructured. The residue is worldview: Whittemore reads demand as real and lagging supply, so the fight is distributive and therefore winnable; Zitron reads demand as manufactured by two funded losers, so the fight is about who is left holding an empty shed. Whittemore is vindicated if communities that sign good checklists collect for decades as Loudoun has; Zitron if the first wave of defaults strands towns with derelict plant and stranded grid costs. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: the NDA-shrouded deal structure is indefensible, and communities are bearing risk they cannot see. Watch the occupancy of the first big 2026 sites to switch on.
